clue.text: Our slim jeans altered for chronicler of Hommes de 28

indicators.note: altered means changed, so the letters of these three words are rearranged into a name

explanation.surface: Someone's slim-fitting jeans have been taken in for a French author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altered' rearranges OUR SLIM JEANS. The 28 points to 28-across: Jules Romains wrote the long novel cycle Les Hommes de bonne volonté.
explanation.definitionFit: Romains chronicled French life from 1908 to 1933 in his twenty-seven-volume cycle Les Hommes de bonne volonté.

clue.text: Stephen Crane's girl of the streets

definitions.text: Stephen Crane's girl of the streets

parts.words: Stephen Crane's girl of the streets
parts.note: points to the heroine of Crane's 1893 novella Maggie: A Girl of the Streets, asking for her surname

explanation.walkthrough: The heroine of Crane's novella is Maggie Johnson; the clue wants her family name.
explanation.definitionFit: Maggie, the Bowery girl of Crane's title, bears this surname in the novella.

clue.text: Citadel housed this old French king

explanation.surface: A fortress once sheltered a deposed monarch of France.
explanation.walkthrough: The Citadel is A. J. Cronin's 1937 novel, in which Le Roy is a wealthy businessman among Andrew Manson's London connections; 'le roy' is the old French spelling of 'the king'.
explanation.definitionFit: Le Roy is a character in Cronin's novel The Citadel, and in archaic French 'le roy' meant the monarch, as in the royal assent formula.

clue.text: Maxwell Andersen's children who had to work for a living

definitions.text: Maxwell Andersen's children who had to work for a living

parts.words: Maxwell Andersen's children who had to work for a living
parts.note: names Maxwell Anderson's 1927 play and glosses its title with the nursery rhyme line about the child who works hard for a living

explanation.walkthrough: Anderson's play is Saturday's Children; the title comes from the rhyme 'Monday's child is fair of face', in which Saturday's child works hard for its living.
explanation.definitionFit: The play's title is drawn from the weekday rhyme, where the child born on that day labours for a livelihood.

clue.text: Fleming made a secret of this state of service

definitions.text: Fleming made a secret of this state of service

parts.words: Fleming made a secret of this state of service
parts.note: Ian Fleming's novel On Her Majesty's Secret Service adds 'Secret' to the familiar abbreviation stamped on official British post

explanation.walkthrough: On Her Majesty's Service, abbreviated, was printed on British government mail; Fleming's Bond title inserts 'Secret' into that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The initials stand for On Her Majesty's Service, the official franking on Crown correspondence.

clue.text: He's not there, like Macavity and Lord Clonbrony

explanation.surface: A cat burglar and an Irish peer share the habit of vanishing.
explanation.walkthrough: In T. S. Eliot's poem, 'Macavity's not there' whenever a crime is found; Lord Clonbrony is the landlord who lives away from his Irish estates in Maria Edgeworth's novel The Absentee.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone missing from where they should be, as Eliot's mystery cat always is and as Edgeworth's titled character is from his lands.

clue.text: Early Booker winner had something to answer for

definitions.text: Early Booker winner had something to answer for

parts.words: Early Booker winner had something to answer for
parts.note: the phrase 'something to answer for' sounds like guilt but is the title of the novel that won the first Booker Prize in 1969

explanation.walkthrough: P. H. Newby won the first Booker Prize, in 1969, with Something to Answer For.
explanation.definitionFit: This novelist took the inaugural Booker Prize for his book Something to Answer For.

clue.text: Sleep aid concocted by Ronsard's group

indicators.note: concocted means mixed up like a potion, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sleeping draught is brewed up by a circle of French poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concocted' rearranges SLEEP AID. Ronsard led La Pléiade, the group of seven sixteenth-century French poets named after the star cluster.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pléiade was the poetic circle that Ronsard headed, named after the seven sisters of the star cluster.

clue.text: The luck of Conrad

parts.note: a word for luck that is also the title of Joseph Conrad's 1913 novel

explanation.walkthrough: Conrad's novel Chance (1913) was his first popular success.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortune or luck is the ordinary sense, and Chance is also the title of a Conrad novel.

clue.text: Obdurate newspaper produced by Dickens

parts.note: obdurate means stubborn and unyielding, that is hard
The Times is the London daily newspaper

explanation.surface: A stubborn newspaper's output is credited to Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard Times is the 1854 novel Dickens wrote, set in the industrial Coketown.

clue.text: Apparently a Scottish novelist

parts.note: the joke is that the name suggests someone from Wales, yet it belongs to an Edinburgh writer

explanation.walkthrough: Irvine Welsh, author of Trainspotting, is Scottish though his surname names the people of Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Irvine Welsh is the Edinburgh-born writer of Trainspotting, whose surname points to Wales instead.

clue.text: Whodunit writer speaks about medical drama series

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word is placed around the other

parts.note: speaks means says
ER is the American hospital drama series

explanation.surface: A detective novelist talks about a hospital television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the container signal here, not 'concerning'. ER was the long-running Chicago hospital drama on American television; Dorothy L. Sayers created Lord Peter Wimsey.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy L. Sayers wrote detective fiction featuring Lord Peter Wimsey.

clue.text: The moon sleeps with him, and would not be awaked, said Portia

definitions.text: The moon sleeps with him, and would not be awaked, said Portia

parts.words: The moon sleeps with him, and would not be awaked, said Portia
parts.note: quotes Portia in The Merchant of Venice, Act 5, with the shepherd's name replaced by 'him'

explanation.walkthrough: Portia says 'the moon sleeps with Endymion, And would not be awaked', alluding to the shepherd loved by the moon goddess Selene.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the shepherd beloved by the moon goddess was granted eternal sleep, which Portia's line recalls.

clue.text: David's prophet at Detroit?

parts.note: names the Old Testament seer who rebuked King David, and also the first name that goes before Detroit in Guys and Dolls

explanation.walkthrough: Nathan the prophet confronted David over Bathsheba; Nathan Detroit runs the floating crap game in the musical Guys and Dolls.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the prophet who rebuked King David, and the gambler in Guys and Dolls is called this before his surname Detroit.

clue.text: Fielding's master offers blow followed by hesitation

indicators.note: followed by means the second piece comes after the first

parts.note: a thwack is a heavy blow
um is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A tutor in Fielding delivers a smack and then pauses.
explanation.walkthrough: Thwackum is the brutal tutor of Tom Jones in Fielding's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Thwackum is the flogging schoolmaster who teaches Tom Jones and Blifil in Fielding's novel.

clue.text: Implore Barnaby to admit with bad grace

parts.note: implore means beg
Barnaby Rudge is the title character of the Dickens novel

explanation.surface: Someone pleads with Barnaby to concede a point grudgingly.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnaby Rudge is the simple-minded hero of Dickens's novel about the Gordon Riots.
explanation.definitionFit: To concede something resentfully is to grudge it, a synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Villiers run-through "transpos'd" by Marvell

parts.note: names the 1671 farce by George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham, and Marvell's prose satire whose title adds 'Transpros'd' to it

explanation.walkthrough: Villiers wrote the burlesque The Rehearsal; Marvell's The Rehearsal Transpros'd (1672) borrowed its title. 'run-through' gives the everyday sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A practice performance or run-through, and the title shared by the Villiers farce and Marvell's satire.

clue.text: Dramatist's mutant giant rat

definitions.note: read as 'Dramatist is', the 's linking definition to wordplay

indicators.note: mutant means changed in form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A playwright possesses a monstrous mutated rodent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mutant' rearranges GIANT RAT. Terence Rattigan wrote The Winslow Boy and The Browning Version.
explanation.definitionFit: Terence Rattigan was an English playwright of The Browning Version and The Deep Blue Sea.

clue.text: Wells hero uses gun on bad actor

parts.note: the Lewis gun was a light machine gun of the First World War
a ham is an overacting performer

explanation.surface: A character from Wells turns a weapon on a hopeless performer.
explanation.walkthrough: Love and Mr Lewisham (1900) is H. G. Wells's novel about a young schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Lewisham is the title character of Wells's novel Love and Mr Lewisham.

clue.text: "Honest — bears a lovely face" (Thomas Dekker)

parts.note: the missing word completes the refrain of Dekker's song 'Art thou poor, yet hast thou golden slumbers?'

explanation.walkthrough: Dekker's song from Patient Grissil ends each verse with 'Honest labour bears a lovely face'.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in Dekker's line is filled by the word for work or toil.

clue.text: John Dos Passos's country, once a Japanese province

explanation.surface: An American author's homeland was formerly ruled from Tokyo.
explanation.walkthrough: Dos Passos wrote the novel Chosen Country (1951); Chosen was the name of Korea under Japanese rule, 1910 to 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: Dos Passos titled a novel Chosen Country, and Korea was called Chosen while annexed by Japan.

clue.text: Beautiful maiden multiplies with Irish poet

definitions.text: Beautiful maiden multiplies with Irish poet

parts.note: a nymph is a beautiful young woman or nature spirit
AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George William Russell

explanation.surface: A lovely young woman reproduces alongside a poet from Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines: 'Beautiful maiden multiplies' asks for the plural, and the Latin plural of nympha ends with AE, the signature of the Irish poet George Russell.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin plural form means several lovely maidens or nature spirits, the singular multiplied.

clue.text: A spiteful criticism of Sheridan

parts.note: describes malicious slander behind someone's back and points to the scandalmonger Sir Benjamin in Sheridan's The School for Scandal

explanation.walkthrough: Sir Benjamin Backbite is one of the gossips in Sheridan's comedy The School for Scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: To slander someone in their absence, and the surname of Sheridan's gossiping Sir Benjamin.

clue.text: Article removed from Spanish port for resident of Bag End ()

indicators.note: removed from means the article is taken out of the port's name

parts.note: Bilbao is a port in the Basque Country of northern Spain
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Grammar is struck off at a Spanish harbour on behalf of a Hobbit.
explanation.walkthrough: Bag End is the home of Bilbo Baggins in Tolkien's The Hobbit.
explanation.definitionFit: Bilbo Baggins lives at Bag End in Hobbiton in Tolkien's tales.

clue.text: Smollett character offers a sort of access

explanation.surface: A figure from Smollett offers a kind of way in.
explanation.walkthrough: The Adventures of Roderick Random (1748) is Smollett's first novel; random access is the computing term.
explanation.definitionFit: Roderick of Smollett's picaresque novel, and the computer-memory phrase for reaching any item directly.

clue.text: Spirits like geneva, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be heard spoken

parts.note: geneva is an old name for gin, from the Dutch jenever

explanation.surface: Liquors such as Dutch gin, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives the sound of GIN; the genies of Arabian myth are spelt this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Genies are supernatural beings of Arabian and Islamic lore, a sense of the plural 'spirits'.

clue.text: ", Teuton, Kelt I count them all / My friends and brother souls" (Tennyson) TLS OCTOBER

definitions.text: ", Teuton, Kelt I count them all / My friends and brother souls" (Tennyson)

parts.words: ", Teuton, Kelt I count them all / My friends and brother souls" (Tennyson)
parts.note: the gap begins Tennyson's line from 'Hands All Round', which lists three European peoples

explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held ends with stray text 'TLS OCTOBER' from the page. Tennyson's line runs 'Slav, Teuton, Kelt, I count them all'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names a member of the eastern European peoples, set alongside German and Celt in the poem.

clue.text: "(Trollope's) inestimable merit was a complete appreciation of the — " (James)

definitions.text: "(Trollope's) inestimable merit was a complete appreciation of the — " (James)

parts.words: "(Trollope's) inestimable merit was a complete appreciation of the — " (James)
parts.note: quotes Henry James's 1883 essay on Trollope, praising his feel for ordinary everyday life

explanation.walkthrough: James wrote that Trollope's 'great, his inestimable merit was a complete appreciation of the usual'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means the ordinary and everyday, which James saw as Trollope's strength.

clue.text: Craftsman whose village was deserted

explanation.surface: An artisan whose home settlement was abandoned.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Goldsmith wrote the poem The Deserted Village (1770).
explanation.definitionFit: A worker in precious metal, and the surname of Oliver, author of The Deserted Village.

clue.text: 31 across's eponymous feeling of tortured love (not following French maid)

indicators.note: following means this piece comes after the French maid

parts.note: bonne is French for a maidservant

indicators.note: tortured means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tormented passion that does not pursue a French servant girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tortured' rearranges LOVE and NOT; the 31 across of the original grid is Jules Romains, whose cycle Les Hommes de bonne volonté takes this phrase as its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is French for goodwill, the sentiment named in the title of Romains's cycle.
